Front: Agents (Huyen): give her own example of the bidirectional environment/tools constraint.
Back: Chess: the environment (chess board/rules) limits actions to valid chess moves only - no web search tool makes sense there. Conversely, an agent whose only actions are chess moves is confined to chess-shaped environments - useless for something like stock trading. Environment and tool inventory constrain each other both ways.

Front: Agents (Huyen): why do agents typically need more powerful models than non-agent use cases? Name both reasons.
Back: (1) Compound mistakes: per-step accuracy compounds across steps, e.g. 95% per-step accuracy drops to ~0.95^10 = ~60% over 10 steps. (2) Higher stakes: write actions (database mutation, bank transfers, root access) mean failures have real consequences, not just a wrong prediction.

Front: Agents (Huyen): why is a reflection failure (agent thinks it succeeded when it didn't) more dangerous than a tool-use failure?
Back: A tool-use failure (invalid function, wrong parameters) produces an observable error/exception that monitoring can catch. A reflection failure produces nothing - the agent's own self-evaluation is wrong, so no error signal fires and the corrective loop never triggers; the agent just stops in a false 'done' state. Fix: use a separate evaluator, not the same agent grading its own success.
